claims.text: The initially solid Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu nanoparticles have a homogeneous solid-solution structure at room temperature.
Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu HEA nanoparticles possess intrinsic atomic-scale elemental segregation.
Local elemental segregation produces spatial variations in lattice strain.
Atomic-scale heterogeneity creates regions with locally lower melting temperatures.
Regions with locally lower melting temperatures premelt earlier than the remainder of the particle.
Spatially heterogeneous premelting broadens the overall melting transition.
Chemically uniform monometallic or well-mixed bimetallic nanoparticles exhibit sharper and more spatially homogeneous melting than the HEA nanoparticles.
The HEA nanoparticles will show localized premelting at lower temperatures than comparable baseline nanoparticles.
Localized premelting will be observable through spatial variations in phase contrast and elemental distributions.
The HEA nanoparticles will melt over a wider temperature range than comparable monometallic or well-mixed bimetallic nanoparticles.
Particle size determines whether intrinsic properties or surface effects dominate the phase transition.
Moderate heating and cooling rates permit intrinsic thermal responses to be resolved.
Nanoparticle size, synthesis history, and surface effects may change the observed extent of heterogeneity.
The interaction of heating kinetics and intrinsic thermodynamics may produce variability in the melting range.

contradictions.description: The initial state is described as a homogeneous solid solution, whereas the hypothesis treats local elemental segregation as an intrinsic feature. These can coexist only if 'homogeneous' refers to average phase homogeneity or if segregation develops during heating, neither of which is specified.
